name: misa77
workload: Decompression throughput versus compression ratio on silesia.tar, single thread, trusted-input (unsafe) decoder, compared with lz4, lz4hc, zstd, lzav, snappy, zxc and LZSSE.
claimed_speedup: README: '1.5-3x faster than LZ4 for decompression on x86 and ARM (with better ratios!)'. lzbench 2.4 table: misa77 0.6.0 -1 decompresses at 7813 MB/s versus lz4 1.10.0 at 3832 MB/s (2.04x, derived from page data) at ratio 42.65 versus 47.60; misa77 -3 decompresses at 6470 MB/s versus lz4hc -4 at 3587 MB/s (1.8x, derived from page data) at ratio 37.76 versus 37.65. Compression is much slower (misa77 -1 73.8 MB/s versus lz4 550 MB/s).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary); lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; compile flags not stated on the page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes). The project's own README table (Intel Core i7-14650HX, Apple M3) gives 5376 MB/s versus lz4 2514 MB/s.
stars_or_usage: 172 stars; merged into lzbench and TurboBench
tradeoffs: Slow compression by design (write-once, read-many). Needs a C++20 compiler, little-endian 64-bit only; AVX2/SSE2 chosen at runtime on x86, NEON on ARM. Unsafe decoder has undefined behavior on corrupt input; the safe decoder costs about 3-5% and level 4 has no safe decoder yet.
caveats: Compares against LZ4-class codecs; zstd and zlib are not beaten on ratio. Ratio is worse than lz4hc at some levels. The lzbench table is third-party (lzbench maintainer) but the exact compile flags are not stated. Project is young (0.6.0).
found_via: lzbench README (results table of lzbench 2.4 on EPYC 9555P), reached by browsing registry port lists (vcpkg ports lzfse/liblzf/lzav/isal/libdeflate and crates.io searches) and GitHub topic pages lz77/lz4; also WebSearch 'new LZ77 compressor faster decompression than LZ4 and zstd github C++ lzbench Silesia 2026'

name: LZFSE (Apple reference implementation)
workload: Silesia tar, single-thread in-memory compression and decompression versus zlib at several levels, through lzbench.
claimed_speedup: README: 'targets similar compression rates at higher compression and decompression speed compared to deflate using zlib' (no numbers in the README). lzbench 2.4 table: lzfse 91.1 MB/s compress, 732 MB/s decompress, ratio 31.91; zlib 1.3.2 -6 26.8 MB/s, 314 MB/s, ratio 32.19; zlib -9 11.3 MB/s, 318 MB/s, ratio 31.92. That is about 3.4x faster compression and 2.3x faster decompression than zlib -6 at nearly the same ratio (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary); lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; compile flags not stated on the page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes)
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars; Apple's Compression framework algorithm; vcpkg port lzfse
tradeoffs: Reference C implementation with a command line tool; not tuned for SIMD. Other codecs (zstd -5, libdeflate) give similar or better ratio at higher speed.
caveats: lzbench bundles the 2017-03-08 version. The README itself has no numbers, so the evidence is only the lzbench table. zstd 1.5.7 -5 (126 MB/s, 1172 MB/s, ratio 29.60) beats it on every axis. Last commit 2017.
found_via: vcpkg port list (versions/baseline.json contains lzfse) and the lzbench README table

name: BriefLZ
baseline: zlib (zlib 1.2.11 in the README table, zlib 1.3.2 in lzbench 2.4)
workload: Silesia corpus through lzbench, compression and decompression speed and ratio at several levels, compared with brotli, zstd, zlib, lz4hc and lzo.
claimed_speedup: README table (Core i5-4570 at 3.2 GHz): brieflz 1.3.0 -6 compresses at 17 MB/s and decompresses at 400 MB/s with ratio 31.71; zlib 1.2.11 -9 does 11 MB/s and 320 MB/s with ratio 31.92 (about 1.5x faster compression and 1.25x faster decompression, derived from page data). lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P): brieflz -6 22.8 MB/s and 328 MB/s versus zlib -9 11.3 MB/s and 318 MB/s (2.0x compression, 1.03x decompression, derived).
compiler_and_flags: README table: not stated. lzbench 2.4 table: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary); lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; compile flags not stated on the page
hardware: README table: Core i5-4570 at 3.2 GHz. lzbench 2.4 table (https://github.com/inikep/lzbench): AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes)
tradeoffs: Very small code (compressor 147 lines, decompressor 61 lines); no entropy coding; has no window size limit, so it needs the whole buffer.
caveats: Decompression gain over zlib is marginal (3-25%). The README says its comparison 'is not entirely fair because BriefLZ has no window size limit'. zstd and brotli beat it at similar ratios. Tier B rests on the lzbench 2.4 table in the lzbench repo (third-party); the README table is first-party and lacks compiler flags.
found_via: lzbench README supported-compressor list; opened the brieflz README

name: libbsc
workload: Silesia tar single-thread compression and decompression through lzbench; block-sorting compressor versus xz and bzip2.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4: bsc 3.3.12 -m0 -e1 compresses at 19.4 MB/s with ratio 23.26; xz 5.8.4 -5 compresses at 3.84 MB/s with ratio 23.70 (5.1x faster compression and a smaller output, derived from page data); bzip2 1.0.8 -9 does 12.7 MB/s with ratio 25.75 (1.5x, derived). Decompression is slower: 25.0 MB/s versus xz 121 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary); lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; compile flags not stated on the page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes)
tradeoffs: Compression-side win only; decompression is 5x slower than xz and 50-80x slower than zlib. Optional NVIDIA GPU acceleration. Memory heavy block sorting.
caveats: The README has no benchmark numbers (it points to libbsc.com, not opened). The lzbench build is multithreaded-capable but run single-threaded. Win is against xz and bzip2 compression speed only.
found_via: lzbench README supported-compressor list and results table

name: Brotli
workload: Silesia tar single-thread in-memory compression and decompression through lzbench.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4: brotli 1.2.0 -5 compresses at 53.3 MB/s, decompresses at 419 MB/s, ratio 28.10; zlib 1.3.2 -9 does 11.3 MB/s, 318 MB/s, ratio 31.92 (4.7x faster compression, 1.3x faster decompression and a smaller output, derived from page data). Against xz 5.8.4 -1 (19.2 MB/s, 105 MB/s, ratio 27.75): 2.8x faster compression and 4.0x faster decompression at about 1.3% larger output (derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary); lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; compile flags not stated on the page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes)
stars_or_usage: 14.9k stars; Chromium and web server standard (RFC 7932)
tradeoffs: Highest levels are very slow to compress (-11: 0.56 MB/s). Decompression is slower than zstd (1.5.7 -8: 1301 MB/s) and lz4.
caveats: Brotli is itself a named baseline in this category; the win recorded here is against zlib and xz. Levels were chosen from the lzbench table. The README only links third-party benchmark pages (Squash, LTCB, lzturbo; not opened) and has no numbers of its own.
found_via: lzbench README results table; opened github.com/google/brotli

name: lz4ultra
baseline: lz4 (lz4 1.9.2 -12 high-compression encoder, same LZ4 format)
workload: Decompression time for enwik9 (1,000,000,000 bytes) of LZ4-format streams produced by lz4 -12 versus lz4ultra's optimal packer.
claimed_speedup: README table: lz4ultra 1.3.0 --favor-decSpeed output (376,118,079 bytes) decompresses in 296,972 microseconds versus 457,141 microseconds for lz4 1.9.2 -12 --favor-decSpeed output (377,175,400 bytes), 1.54x faster (derived from page data); favor-ratio output 347,936 versus 505,804 microseconds (1.45x, derived) with 372,443,347 versus 371,680,323 compressed bytes.
hardware: Core i7-6700 (as printed in the README table)
tradeoffs: Output is plain LZ4 format, readable by the standard lz4 decoder; the gain comes from fewer tokens, not from a faster decoder. Compression is an offline optimal parse and slower than lz4 -12 (no timing given).
caveats: First-party numbers, one dataset, no compiler flags, and the README does not say which decoder produced the timings (it says its own decompressor is not as optimized as lz4 proper). Compared against lz4 1.9.2 (2019), not the current 1.10.0. CC0 matchfinder carries no patent grant.
found_via: GitHub topics page lz4 (C++), then lz4ultra README

name: ACEAPEX
workload: Parallel decode of a 1 GB FASTQ file (ERR194147) with block-independent LZ77 and absolute offsets; also enwik9 and silesia, on CPU with 8 threads and on GPU.
claimed_speedup: README: 'At ratio 3.98 versus zstd -3 at 3.96 on the same file, ACEAPEX -T8 decodes at 7,401 MB/s against zstd -3 at 2,026 MB/s: 3.65x faster at genuinely comparable ratio.' Single thread decode is 1,624 MB/s on that file. lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P, silesia.tar) lists aceapex 1.0.1 -1 at 55.9 MB/s compress, 675 MB/s decompress, ratio 32.35 versus zlib 1.3.2 -9 at 11.3 MB/s, 318 MB/s, ratio 31.92.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -std=c++17 (CPU build); nvcc -O3 (GPU build); links libzstd for entropy
hardware: README says reproduce scripts were verified on an EPYC 4344P; the CPU for the FASTQ table is not stated there. GPU numbers on Tesla T4 to Blackwell.
stars_or_usage: 6 stars; included in lzbench 2.3/2.4 and TurboBench 2.2.1
tradeoffs: Encode is slow and research grade; the ratio is 1.2-1.55x worse than zstd -19 on FASTQ. Main CPU build depends on libzstd; one GPU mode needs the closed-source nvcomp library. Block independence enables random access and GPU decode.
caveats: First-party claim, mostly genomic data. The 3.65x figure compares an 8-thread decoder with zstd -3 whose thread count is not stated; single thread (1,624 MB/s) is slower than zstd -3 on the same file. The README previously published higher figures from a sample with degenerate quality strings and re-measured them. Papers are on arXiv (not opened).
found_via: GitHub topics page lz77 (C++) and the lzbench README compressor list

name: AOCL-Compression
baseline: zlib; also bzip2, snappy, zstd, lz4, xz/lzma upstream implementations
workload: Silesia corpus (211.9 MB tar), single core pinned to CPU 0, five runs; AMD-tuned builds of seven codecs compared with the stock lzbench builds.
claimed_speedup: From lzbench pull request 321 (AOCL-Compression 5.3.0): zlib up to 3.7x faster compression and 2x faster decompression; bzip2 2.1-2.3x compression and +60-69% decompression; snappy +20% compression and 2x decompression; zstd +14-21% and +8-10%; lz4hc +18% compression; lzma +12% and +17%; lz4 +5% and +2%, with minor ratio trade-offs.
license: BSD-3-Clause AND MIT AND NCSA (file-by-file per LICENSE.txt)
tradeoffs: Tuned for AMD Zen with dynamic dispatch (SSE2 to AVX512); minor compression ratio loss in fast modes; one API for LZ4, zlib, zstd, bzip2, snappy, lzma. Vendors modified copies of the upstream codecs.
caveats: Numbers come from percentages in an open pull request description written by the vendor (the maintainer raised build and correctness concerns), not from raw MB/s; the repo README has no numbers. Licensing is per file and was not audited. The IEEE paper on it was not opened (blocked). Gains on zstd and lz4 are small.
found_via: WebSearch 'AOCL-Compression performance gain over upstream zlib lz4 zstd bzip2 speedup Zen EPYC' after GitHub topics page data-compression (C)

name: miniz
workload: Single-source-file zlib/Deflate implementation; positioned between fast real-time compressors and zlib.
claimed_speedup: README: 'at levels 2-9, miniz.c is designed to compare favorably against zlib's ratio and speed'; at level 1 it 'compresses around 5-9% better than minilzo, but is approx. 35% slower'. No zlib numbers are given on the page.
stars_or_usage: 2.9k stars; vcpkg and Conan port; used widely for PNG and ZIP
tradeoffs: Single threaded; single file; zlib-compatible API subset; includes PNG writer and ZIP reader/writer.
caveats: Claim has no numbers against zlib; the README refers to a performance comparison page that was not opened. Newer zlib forks (zlib-ng, libdeflate) are faster. Tier D entry, kept for notability.
found_via: vcpkg versions/baseline.json (port miniz) and Conan center recipe list; opened the miniz README

name: lbzip2 (maintained fork)
workload: Silesia tar through lzbench, lbzip2 run single-threaded in bzip2 format; the tool also has a multithreaded mode.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4: lbzip2 2.6.5 -1 compresses at 22.0 MB/s and decompresses at 62.7 MB/s versus bzip2 1.0.8 -1 at 13.5 MB/s and 41.1 MB/s (1.6x and 1.5x, derived from page data); -9: 22.4 and 47.0 versus 12.7 and 35.5 MB/s with the same output size class (ratio 25.75 for both). Fork README: about 8% faster compression and 9% faster decompression than lbzip2 2.5 (2015) on 220 MB of mixed data on an Apple M5 Max, single thread.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary); lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; compile flags not stated on the page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes)
stars_or_usage: 1 star (fork); upstream kjn/lbzip2 has 156 stars and is unmaintained
tradeoffs: Command line tool, output stays bzip2 compatible; real gains come from multiple threads (not shown in the lzbench multithreaded table). Not a library API; GPL-3.0.
caveats: Baseline bzip2 is not in this category's list. The fork was created on 2026-08-17 from upstream commit 724352c and is one person's work. Gain in the lzbench table is a single-thread comparison.
found_via: lzbench README supported-compressor list (lbzip2 2.6.5 linked to caius72/lbzip2)
